title: Mudgala turns down heaven
hookLine: a poor sage is offered a chariot to heaven, asks one question, and says no
carry: heaven isn't the goal; freedom is
tomorrow: a king waits one song, and ages pass
last: MASTER THE SENSES BY OFFERING THEM.

lines: A SAGE WHO LIVES ON GLEANINGS.
cards: In the Mahabharata, Vyasa tells Yudhishthira about a sage named Mudgala, who is poor on purpose.
He lives by gleaning, picking up the grain left in the fields after harvest, and every two weeks he cooks what he's gathered and feeds whoever comes to his door.

Then the well known for it, short-tempered sage Durvasa starts showing up, again and again, eating every last grain and smearing the leftovers on himself. Mudgala goes hungry, and never once gets angry.
So heaven sends a chariot for him. A divine messenger at the door: get in.

teach.h: MUDGALA ASKS: WHAT'S WRONG WITH HEAVEN?
teach.b: Mudgala doesn't get in. First he asks: what's heaven like, and what's wrong with it? The messenger is honest.
Heaven is lovely: no hunger, no age, music, fine company. But there you only enjoy what you've already earned; you can't do any new good. You see others shining brighter than you.

And when your merit runs out, you fall. So Mudgala sends the chariot away and turns to meditation, toward a place with no grief and no falling, and the story says he reached it. Here's the Hindu teaching, plainly.

teach.h: SVARGA IS A STOP. MOKSHA IS THE GOAL.
teach.b: Heaven, svarga, is real, but it isn't the goal. It's a reward, and rewards run out. Krishna says it in the Gita: people enjoy the wide world of heaven, and when their merit is spent, they come back.
The goal is moksha, freedom, which doesn't run out.
Patanjali says it in yoga's terms. Sutra 3.49: full discernment brings knowing everything.

teach.h: HEAVEN ISN'T THE GOAL; FREEDOM IS.
teach.b: Sutra 3.50: let go even of that, and freedom comes. Sutra 3.51: when those in high places invite you, don't cling and don't be proud, or the old trouble comes back.
The classical commentary acts it out: gods arrive with chariots and an elixir against age, and the yogi says no. Notice the danger is the good stuff. Nobody needs a warning against misery.

It's why Prahlada, offered any boon he liked, said that serving God for a reward makes you a trader, not a devotee. A Hindu can be glad of good things, a prize, praise, a raise, and still say: that isn't the point.

how: Hindus pray and work for good things, but the tradition teaches that heaven (svarga) is a reward that runs out and moksha is the goal; devotees remember saints like Prahlada, who were offered boons and asked for nothing but God.

o: being clever enough to win every debate
a sixth sense for danger before it comes

games.q: heaven and freedom — tap the pairs.
p: heaven: real, and it runs out

s: in Hinduism, heaven is the final goal
svarga is a reward that runs out; the goal is moksha, freedom.
Mudgala asked about heaven's faults before saying no
the messenger named them: no new good there, envy of others, and a fall when merit runs out.
refusing proudly is fine, as long as you refuse
3.51 warns against clinging and against pride.

games.q: a divine messenger offers you heaven for all your good deeds. what would Mudgala ask first?
games.why: he asked about heaven's faults: merit runs out and you fall. so he chose moksha, which doesn't. sutra 3.51 adds: say no without clinging and without pride.

practice: Rest on the breath until something pleasant invites you away: a daydream, a plan, a drowsy warmth. Treat it like Mudgala's chariot. Notice it, thank it, don't get in.

If you pray, let a name of God be how you come back: Ram, Krishna, Om namah Shivaya. If you don't, just come back to the breath. And if a little pride follows at having stayed, send that chariot away too.

wordCard.voice: Omniscience. Knowing everything, which Patanjali says comes from full discernment, and which he says to set down too, the way Mudgala set down heaven.

orig.note: Sanskrit mokṣa: release, freedom; the goal Mudgala chose over svarga, heaven.

carryVoice: Your line: heaven isn't the goal; freedom is. Mudgala sent the chariot away. Rest well.
